questiontext.text:
Write down two equations in the form \(ax+by=c\) such that when you try to solve them simultaneously there are no solutions.

Equation (1) [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]

Equation (2) [[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]]

\({@ans2@} \quad \) Equation (2)

we can see that they intersect. The \(x\) and \(y\) coordinates of the intersection point are the solutions to these equations.

{@plot([plot_ans1,plot_ans2],[x,xmin,xmax],[y,ymin,ymax], [box, false], [yx_ratio, 1], [axes,solid], [xtics, xmin+1, 1, xmax-1],[ytics, ymin+1, 1, ymax-1],grid2d,[legend,"Equation 1", "Equation 2"])@}

truefeedback.text: Good thinking, but there are actually infinitely many solutions to these simultaneous equations. Graphically they correspond to the equation of the same line.

falsefeedback.text:
If we plot the two equations that you gave as an answer

\({@ans1@} \quad \) Equation (1)

\({@ans2@} \quad \) Equation (2)

we can see that they do not intersect. This means that there are no solutions to the equations.

{@plot([plot_ans1,plot_ans2],[x,xmin,xmax],[y,ymin,ymax], [box, false], [yx_ratio, 1], [axes,solid], [xtics, xmin+1, 1, xmax-1],[ytics, ymin+1, 1, ymax-1],grid2d,[legend,"Equation 1", "Equation 2"])@}

Worked solution:

Here is an example of two equations such that when you try to solve them simultaneously there are no solutions:

\({@eq1@} \quad \) Equation (1)

\({@eq2@}\quad \) Equation (2)

Indeed, when you try to solve simultaneously by subtracting equation (1) from equation (2), you get

\({@eq2-eq1@}. \)

This is not true, so there are no solutions.

Graphically, if we plot these two straight lines, we can see that there are no solutions because the lines are parallel.

{@plot([line1,line2],[x,-4,4],[y,-2,5], [box, false], [yx_ratio, 1], [axes, solid], [xtics, -3, 1, 3],[ytics, -1, 1, 4],grid2d,[legend,"Equation 1", "Equation 2"])@}

Any two lines that are parallel will have no solutions.

Two lines are parallel if they have the same gradient. If the coefficients of \(x\) and \(y\) are the same in both equations, as in (1) and (2) above, then the gradients will be the same. The same holds true also when the coefficients of \(x\) and \(y\) are are in the same ratio, for example

\({@eq1@}\)

\({@expand(3*lhs(eq2))=rhs(eq1)+1@}\).

Note also that the constants in the two equations should not be equal or in the same ratio as the coefficients of \(x\) and \(y\). Indeed in this case the two equations would correspond to the same line and there would be infinitely many solutions.

falsefeedback.text: Equation 1 is not in the correct form.
